content: To describe tuberculosis (TB) interventions effectively, it is essential to have a clear understanding of the intervention's coverage and objectives. This can be determined by specific intervention targets or recent epidemiological data. For example, in passive case finding (PCF), the process includes diagnostic visits, diagnostic tests, and patient support activities. These may involve tests, treatment protocols, drug regimens, contact tracing, follow-up, mobile health (M-health) tools, or infection control equipment and supplies. Vaccination against TB primarily involves the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, which is administered to infants, children, and young adults (typically between 8 and 18 years old) to prevent TB. The vaccination intervention also includes treatment for adverse reactions, such as liver function monitoring or managing peripheral neuropathy. Passive case finding (PCF) is the standard method for detecting TB cases. It involves individuals with TB symptoms presenting themselves at public or private health facilities, where a healthcare worker assesses them and orders diagnostic tests. Technologies used in PCF vary depending on the setting and patient characteristics. These include verbal symptom screening, cough triage, sputum induction, Xpert® MTB/RIF, microscopy (LED or Ziehl-Neelsen), culture (solid or liquid), chest X-rays (film or digital), rapid HIV tests, line probe assays (LPA) for firstand second-line drugs, drug sensitivity testing (DST), lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM), interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), tuberculin skin tests (TST), fine needle biopsies, bronchial and gastric lavage, and imaging for extra-pulmonary TB (EPTB) such as CT scans or ultrasounds. Additional tests may include HIV confirmatory tests, CD4 counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, full blood counts, liver function tests, creatinine levels, and glucose monitoring. Intensified case finding (ICF) targets high-risk populations, such as people living with HIV, individuals with diabetes, or those attending maternal and child health clinics. It uses technologies like symptom screening, X-rays, and Xpert® MTB/RIF, and may incorporate other PCF technologies. ICF activities include screening visits, diagnostic tests, and patient support, with costs calculated for each activity. Active case finding (ACF) involves screening and diagnosing TB in populations not typically detected through PCF. This includes household contacts, urban poor populations, prisoners, mobile and migrant populations, and healthcare workers at occupational risk. ACF may use fewer technologies than PCF, such as verbal symptom screening, Xpert® MTB/RIF, microscopy, X-rays, and rapid HIV tests. It can be conducted in various settings, including mobile clinics, schools, prisons, or households. TB treatment encompasses all activities related to managing active TB cases, including observation, patient support, quality-of-life restoration, relapse prevention, and reducing transmission. Treatment is provided during intensive and continuation phases and can occur in households, communities, public or private facilities, or specialized TB hospitals. It includes first-, second-, and third-line drug regimens, palliative care, monitoring for treatment response and adverse events, nutritional assessments, and tracing patients lost to follow-up. HIV-positive patients may also receive antiretroviral therapy (ART) and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. TB prevention focuses on screening and treating latent and active TB among children and HIV-positive adults. Technologies include symptom screening, IGRA or TST tests, and treatment protocols such as six months of isoniazid (6H), lifelong isoniazid, or three months of once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine (3HP). ART regimens and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis are also part of prevention strategies. Infection control in TB involves minimizing transmission risks in health facilities, laboratories, congregate settings, and households. Above-site TB program services include activities at the national level, such as strategic planning, program reviews, training, advocacy, procurement, and quality assurance. These services are delivered through ministries of health, national TB programs, public and private health facilities, and non-governmental organizations. Costs for these activities are calculated based on unit costs per recipient or intervention. These costs include direct and ancillary expenses for services such as vaccination, case finding, treatment, and prevention. Costing guidelines also emphasize the importance of defining the scope of inputs, time horizons, and methods for estimating resource use.
